Angle Property

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Drag the dots and watch the green circle turn into the red one while the two slanted lines keep the same tilt.
How to play: Drag O, S, P, R or T with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and press the arrow keys. Tick "Show names" to label the crossing dots, or "Hint" to draw the slanted lines.
Look for the math

This picture turns a circle inside out. Every point hops along a line through the centre O, yet the tilt of the lines that cross the circle does not change. Drag a dot and watch the two angle readings: they move together and stay equal.

Every point hops along a line through O

In inversion in a circle of radius R, a point X and its image X′ lie on the same ray from O and satisfy OX × OX′ = R². A circle that misses O becomes another circle; a circle that passes through O becomes a straight line. Two circles touching at O become parallel lines, and two circles crossing at O become crossing lines with the same angle. The logic test checked all four statements on hundreds of circles. The applet switches to the straight-line picture when |OP² − r²| ≤ 100; that drawing tolerance is kept here.

Why the angles stay the same

Let P and Q go to P′ and Q′. Since OP × OP′ = OQ × OQ′ = R², triangles OPQ and OQ′P′ are similar. The turn at O is the same and the sides around it scale the same way, so the angle where a line meets a circle is copied to where it meets the image circle. Maps with this property are called conformal or isogonal. The green and red tangent lines in the hint make equal angles with OT in every tested position, to within a billionth of a degree.

A formula for every pair of points

The similarity gives P′Q′ = R² × PQ / (OP × OQ). If the inversion is followed by a reflection, its power k is negative and the same rule becomes P′Q′ = |k| × PQ / (OP × OQ). Both formulae were checked on hundreds of random triples of points. The old applet offered only a positive power, so the negative case is checked in the code test but has no control on this page.

Homologous and antihomologous dots

Any two circles can be inverted into one another: take a centre of homothety of the two circles as O and choose the power to match the sizes. The applet's red circle is a homothetic copy of the green one as well as its inverse. Along the line OT the dots pair in two ways: A and B′ are homologous (joined by the homothety), while A and A′ are antihomologous (joined by the inversion). Both pairings were checked over the whole sample.

Tick Hint, drag T until the line cuts both circles, then drag S: the two angle readings change together but never differ. Now pull R towards O until the green circle passes through it and watch its red image become a straight line.
